klo: Articulate performance expectations that are clear, strategically relevant and consistent with enterprise outcomes.
Evaluate the readiness of individuals and teams to fulfil their strategic responsibilities.
Recognise the contribution relationships and dependencies that influence organisational performance.
Demonstrate shared ownership and mutual accountability for agreed results.

sections.label: Facilitator Guide
sections.sub: Use this tab to orient yourself before each section. It contains purpose, tone, key facilitation questions, and watch points for the full unit.

guidance: ◆ Unit Intent

Unit 7 addresses the single most common reason strategy fails at the human level: expectations are communicated but never truly established. The distinction is subtle in language and profound in execution impact. The unit moves leaders from announcing targets to securing genuine ownership. The Alignment Dialogue (Score → Evaluate → Resolve) is the centrepiece tool — practical, immediate, and directly applicable.
This unit is highly experiential. The role-play in Application is essential: it is where the conceptual work becomes a skill. Protect the time for it.
◆ Key Facilitation Questions
“If you distributed your team’s scorecard right now — without conversation, without context — how many of them would genuinely own those targets?”
“Think of the last time a delivery goal was missed. Was the expectation set — or was it established?”
“Who in your expectations chain could derail delivery — and have you had the alignment conversation with them?”
“When someone on your team gives you a 6 out of 10 on alignment — what does your instinct tell you to do? And what should you do?”
◆ Tone & Watch Points

Watch for: leaders who confuse clarity with alignment. A person can understand an expectation perfectly and still not own it. Probe: “Clarity tells you they heard it. Alignment tells you they’ll deliver it. How do you know the difference?”
Watch for: leaders who treat the Alignment Score as a report card. The score is a diagnostic. If someone gives a 6, the leader’s job is to understand it and resolve it.
Application: Run the role-play with real expectations from participants’ current contexts where possible. The closer the scenario is to their actual work, the more transferable the skill.

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Naming the distinction between setting and establishing expectations — and the two mechanisms that close the gap between a delivery goal and genuine ownership.
slo: Articulate expectations that are clear, consistent with enterprise outcomes and supported by the contributors they depend on.
Evaluate whether individuals have the clarity, capability and commitment to own an expectation.

parts.title: 1.1 — Setting vs Establishing Expectations
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Open with the script question: “If you distributed your team’s scorecard right now — without conversation, without context — how many of them would genuinely own those targets?” Let the silence sit. Most leaders will realise their answer is “fewer than I thought.” That discomfort is the entry point for the rest of the unit.
content: The difference between setting expectations and establishing expectations is subtle in language and profound in execution impact. It determines whether a performance target becomes an instruction that people comply with or a commitment that people own.
Execution begins when the people responsible for those goals internalise the expectation and accept ownership of the result.
Dimension
Setting Expectations
Establishing Expectations
Approach | Top-down declaration; target communicated and assigned | Leadership alignment process; result defined and ownership secured
Focus | Clarity of instruction | Mutual readiness for execution
Dialogue | Limited; assumption that understanding = commitment | Structured; tests feasibility, surfaces constraints, secures commitment
Execution dynamic | Compliance-driven; cautious behaviour, upward escalation | Commitment-driven; initiative, proactive risk surfacing, solving
Result | KPI as metric to be monitored | KPI as personal leadership promise
Accountability | Conditional; defensive ownership | Personal; proactive ownership of the outcome

parts.title: 1.2 — The Three Conditions of Established Expectations
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Most leaders overestimate how much Clarity they have provided and underestimate how little Commitment they have secured. The conversation usually sounds complete to the leader and feels incomplete to the team member. Ask: “After your last expectations conversation, which of the three conditions did you explicitly verify? Clarity — probably. Capability — sometimes. Commitment — almost never.”
content: When expectations are properly established, three conditions are simultaneously present. All three must be confirmed before execution begins. A KPI becomes a personal leadership promise only when all three are in place.
Condition 1
Clarity — The individual understands exactly what success looks like

Clarity means understanding the full picture of the expected outcome: what must be delivered, by when, at what standard, and how success will be recognised. Most expectation conversations stop at the number. Establishing expectations requires confirming that both parties share the same picture of the result.
Facilitation test: “Ask someone on your team to describe what success looks like for their key result. If the description differs from yours, clarity has not yet been established.”
Condition 2
Capability — The system can realistically support delivery

Capability in this context refers to the individual’s skill and to the system surrounding them. Can the organisation actually support delivery of this expectation? Are the resources, decisions, cross-functional dependencies, and coordination mechanisms in place? A person may fully understand and deeply want to own a target that the current system cannot deliver. Establishing expectations surfaces this before execution begins.
Condition 3
Commitment — The person consciously accepts ownership of the outcome

Commitment is the moment the expectation crosses from instruction to promise. The individual accepts personal responsibility for ensuring the outcome is delivered. This cannot be assumed from nodding agreement or email confirmation. It must be actively tested through dialogue. The Alignment Dialogue is the mechanism designed to confirm this transition has occurred.
The Alignment Dialogue asks: “On a scale of 1–10, how aligned are you with the expectation for you to deliver this outcome?” A score below 9 means Commitment is not yet established.

parts.title: 1.3 — The Expectations Chain
parts.meta: Mapping who else influences the outcome
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Ask leaders to pick one current key result and map their Expectations Chain on the spot — 3 minutes, three columns. Then ask: “Have you had an alignment dialogue with everyone in that chain? Or only with the person holding the KPI?” Most will realise they have had the conversation with one person and assumed the rest of the chain would follow. That assumption is where most execution gaps begin.
content: Very few delivery goals are achieved by a single person acting alone. Most results depend on a network of decisions, resources, and coordination across the organisation. The Expectations Chain identifies everyone whose work directly affects the delivery of a Key Result or KPI.

Mapping the Expectations Chain is a critical step before establishing expectations with any individual. It ensures that the KPI is not treated as an isolated personal obligation — and surfaces the dependencies that will determine whether delivery is possible.
Upline Chain
Who
Individuals the leader depends on for approval, decisions, or resources
Examples
Executive leadership, board members, executive sponsors, budget holders
Key question
Who must approve or resource this outcome for delivery to be possible?
Downline Chain
Who
Individuals responsible for executing the work required to achieve the KPI
Examples
Direct reports, project teams, cross-functional collaborators, shared service functions
Key question
Who must deliver specific activities for this outcome to be achieved?
External Chain
Who
External actors whose contributions influence delivery success
Examples
Suppliers, service partners, contractors, regulatory bodies, technology vendors
Key question
Which external actors influence whether this outcome can be delivered?

parts.title: 1.4 — The Alignment Dialogue
parts.meta: Testing whether the expectation is owned
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
Introduce the Alignment Dialogue as a leadership safety system. “You are asking for the score so you can help. A 10 means go. Anything below 10 means there is still work for you to do as the leader.”
content: With the Expectations Chain mapped, the leader conducts an Alignment Dialogue with the individuals responsible for delivering the OKR/KPI. This is a structured conversation designed to test whether the expectation has moved from instruction to commitment.

The Alignment Dialogue uses a simple scale of 1–10. A score of 9 or 10 indicates genuine ownership of delivery. Anything lower demands further deliberation through the Score → Evaluate → Resolve sequence.

The power of the Alignment Dialogue lies in what the number reveals. A score of 6 is data: there is something unresolved between the expectation and the person’s readiness to own it. The leader’s job is to find it and resolve it before execution begins.

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: Why Establishing Expectations Determines Execution Outcomes
sections.sub: Understanding the behavioural mechanisms through which expectation alignment drives ownership, reduces ambiguity, surfaces constraints, and transforms accountability from formal obligation to personal commitment.
slo: Explain how establishing expectations builds ownership and mutual accountability.
Recognise how engagement and accountability degrade when expectations are only communicated.

parts.title: 2.1 — Compliance vs Commitment: The Execution Dynamic
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Invite leaders to locate their current team: “If you are honest — when your team hits an obstacle, what happens first? Do they solve it, or do they escalate it? The answer tells you whether you have compliance or commitment.” This is a signal about whether expectations were established.
content: Strategy is ultimately delivered through human commitment. The moment when expectations are clarified between leader and contributor is the moment a performance target transitions from organisational intention to personal responsibility. If that transition does not occur, execution becomes fragile regardless of how well the system has been designed.
Dimension
△ Compliance-Driven
△ Commitment-Driven
How it looks | Expectations communicated as instructions; acknowledged but not owned | Expectations established through dialogue; owned
Behaviour pattern | Wait for direction; escalate problems upward; focus on reporting | Anticipate risks earlier; coordinate across functions actively; invest effort in solving obstacles
When obstacles arise | Remain cautious; protect reporting; defer resolution to leadership | Take initiative; surface issues early; co-design solutions with the leader
Accountability | Activity ownership: responsible for completing tasks | Outcome ownership: personally accountable for the final result
Energy | Reserved; discretionary effort withheld | Fully invested; discretionary effort freely given

parts.title: 2.2 — Five Mechanisms: Why Expectation Alignment Determines Outcomes
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Ask participants to identify which mechanism is most absent in their current execution environment. “Is your team unclear on what success looks like (Mechanism 2)? Are constraints surfacing too late (Mechanism 3)? Or is accountability diffuse — everyone feels responsible and no one is (Mechanism 4)?” The diagnosis shapes the intervention.
content: Mechanism 1
From Instruction to Ownership

When expectations are merely communicated, people interpret them as instructions. The individual understands what must be achieved but does not yet feel personally accountable for ensuring the outcome is delivered. Establishing expectations through structured dialogue moves the individual from acknowledging the requirement to accepting ownership of the result. This is the fundamental shift that makes execution commitment-driven.
Mechanism 2
Reducing Interpretation Ambiguity

Even when strategic objectives are clearly articulated, individuals often interpret what success requires differently depending on their role, expertise, and operational context. Without structured expectation alignment, people may pursue the same goal while working from different assumptions. Establishing expectations creates a shared interpretation of: what must be delivered, why the result matters, and how success will be recognised. This reduces confusion and allows teams to move forward with greater coordination.
Mechanism 3
Surfacing Constraints Before Execution Begins

Most organisational results require coordination across functions, access to resources, timely decision-making, and cooperation from multiple contributors. If these dependencies are not identified during the expectation conversation, they only become visible later — often when deadlines are already approaching. Establishing expectations allows leaders and contributors to identify these factors early, ensuring required resources are understood, cross-functional dependencies are visible, and potential risks are recognised before they become execution crises.
Mechanism 4
Strengthening Accountability

Accountability is strongest when individuals perceive that the expectations placed on them are clear, achievable, and meaningful. When these conditions are present, people are far more likely to take ownership of outcomes and sustain effort when challenges arise. Establishing expectations strengthens accountability by ensuring both the leader and contributor share a common understanding of: the responsibility involved, what support will be available, what constraints must be addressed, and what standards will be used to evaluate success. This mutual clarity transforms accountability from a formal obligation into a shared commitment.
Mechanism 5
Building the Behavioural Foundation

Strategy execution is fundamentally a behavioural challenge. Plans, metrics, and dashboards provide direction and visibility, but outcomes are ultimately produced through the daily decisions and actions of people. Establishing performance expectations ensures that individuals are psychologically prepared to take responsibility for doing it. When this foundation is in place: individuals understand the purpose behind the work, confidence in feasibility increases, collaboration improves, and accountability becomes proactive.

parts.title: 2.3 — Engagement & Accountability: The Two Casualties
parts.meta: What breaks down when expectations are only set
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

The paradox in the Accountability card is often a moment of recognition for leaders. Name it explicitly: “Have you ever been in a review where everyone has a reason, and no one has an answer? That is diluted accountability in action. It happened because ownership was never established.”
content: When expectations are set without being established, two organisational conditions degrade in a predictable sequence.
First Casualty
Engagement Weakens — Observable but Subtle

When leaders communicate expectations without alignment dialogue, individuals may understand what is required but do not feel personally involved in shaping how the outcome will be delivered. The expectation is acknowledged cognitively but not internalised behaviourally. Work continues and progress may still be visible, but the energy becomes uneven.
Discretionary effort is limited — people do only what is assigned
Individuals wait for direction and leave emerging problems unaddressed
Cross-functional coordination slows because people focus primarily on their own responsibilities
Engagement becomes transactional — people perform their roles but the deeper sense of collective ownership does not materialise
The signal: work is happening, but energy is not invested. People are present but not propelled.
Critical Long-Term Impact
Accountability Dilutes — The Deeper Organisational Cost

The most significant long-term consequence is in the quality of accountability. When expectations are set without alignment, individuals may feel responsible for carrying out activities but not for the final organisational result. Activity ownership and outcome ownership become blurred.
Performance discussions revolve around explanations
Conversations focus on constraints: resources, dependencies, external conditions
Cross-functional dependencies create delays because responsibility for resolving them is unclear
Accountability becomes dispersed: multiple teams feel partially responsible, none fully accountable

The paradox: teams appear to be working hard, meetings are frequent, updates are detailed — yet the organisation consistently struggles to achieve what it set out to deliver. The issue is that ownership of the outcome was assigned without being secured.

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.h2: Where Does the Expectations Gap Emerge?
sections.sub: Examining how each executive function’s natural tendency creates patterns of setting expectations without establishing them — and where the gap most commonly breaks engagement and accountability at scale.
slo: Identify where each executive function tends to set expectations without securing ownership.
Recognise when surface agreement masks unresolved ownership.

parts.title: 3.1 — The Alignment Brigade: CXO Expectation Tendencies & Gaps
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Ask participants to work through their own role first, then two adjacent roles. Key question: “What is the most important expectation you have set — but not yet established — with someone in your expectations chain? What would it take to establish it properly?”
content: Each CXO role naturally focuses on the mechanisms it controls: strategy signals, financial targets, operational processes, culture frameworks, technology milestones, or governance rules. This functional expertise produces a characteristic tendency in how expectations are communicated — and a characteristic gap in how they are established. Click a role to explore its tendency and gap.
CEO
Enterprise Ambition
CFO
Financial Precision
COO
Operational Discipline
CHRO
Cultural Alignment
CTO/CIO
Technical Milestones
CMO
Market Performance
CCO
Commercial Ambition
CPO
Procurement Discipline
CRO
Risk Governance
CSO
Strategic Planning
Typical Tendency

Often sets enterprise ambition and directional expectations, assuming functional leaders will translate these into delivery realities. The strategic signal is clear, but the conditions required for execution may not always be fully established through dialogue.
Expectation Gap

Functional leaders may receive the strategic direction clearly yet lack confirmed ownership of the conditions required for delivery. The assumption that strategic clarity cascades automatically into execution commitment is the CEO’s most common expectation gap.
Typical Tendency

Frequently sets precise financial performance expectations through budgets, targets, and reporting timelines. Financial clarity is strong, yet the cross-functional conditions required to deliver financial outcomes may not always be fully established with the teams responsible for operational delivery.
Expectation Gap

The finance number is clear; the ownership of delivering it is not. Teams understand the financial target but may not have confirmed the cross-functional conditions — resources, decisions, operational capacity — required to achieve it.
Typical Tendency

Commonly sets operational expectations through processes, service levels, and execution discipline. Operational clarity is high, though the broader alignment conversations that build emotional commitment and shared ownership across teams may receive less attention.
Expectation Gap
Process compliance is achieved; outcome ownership is not. Teams follow the operational procedure without necessarily feeling personally responsible for whether the broader result is delivered.
Typical Tendency

Often sets expectations around people behaviour, engagement, and cultural alignment. The dialogue is typically strong on social and emotional commitment, while the direct linkage to operational and commercial delivery expectations may sometimes require further clarification.
Expectation Gap
People feel culturally aligned but may not have clear delivery commitments. Engagement is high; the connection between that engagement and measurable commercial outcomes may remain under-established.
Typical Tendency

Frequently sets delivery expectations through technical specifications, system milestones, and project timelines. Technical clarity is strong, though broader organisational alignment around how technology outcomes enable business delivery may require deeper dialogue.
Expectation Gap

The technical milestone is clear; the business owner’s commitment to using the technology outcome to deliver the result is not established. Technology delivers; business ownership of the enabled result is assumed without confirmation.
Typical Tendency

Often sets market growth or brand performance expectations through campaign metrics and positioning targets. These expectations frequently depend on multiple functions for delivery, yet the cross-functional support commitments required may not always be fully established.
Expectation Gap

The campaign target is clear; the operational and commercial functions have not confirmed their ownership of enabling the marketing outcome. Market expectations are set with marketing; the expectations chain extending to other functions remains under-established.
Typical Tendency

Commonly sets ambitious commercial expectations to drive revenue momentum and market urgency. The stretch targets are clear, although the operational conditions required to sustain those outcomes may not always be fully aligned across the organisation.
Expectation Gap

The commercial target is understood; the operational capacity to deliver it sustainably is not confirmed. Revenue commitments are made without fully establishing whether the organisation’s operational expectations chain has been aligned to support them.
Typical Tendency

Often sets procurement expectations through contractual terms, supplier metrics, and compliance frameworks. These mechanisms create discipline with external partners, though the internal alignment required to convert procurement outcomes into enterprise value may need further establishment.
Expectation Gap

Supplier expectations are clear; internal expectations for converting supplier performance into business value are not established. Procurement delivers inputs; the internal expectations chain for converting those inputs into outcomes remains under-confirmed.
Typical Tendency

Frequently sets expectations for risk control and compliance through governance frameworks, policies, and reporting standards. The rules are clear, yet the deeper organisational ownership of risk-aware behaviour may require additional dialogue to move beyond procedural compliance.
Expectation Gap

The governance rule is understood; the ownership of risk-aware behaviour remains procedural. Compliance is achieved; commitment to risk-aware decision-making as a shared organisational responsibility is not established.
Typical Tendency

Often sets expectations around planning milestones, strategic reviews, and OKR cycles. Strategic process discipline is strong, though the expectations for day-to-day execution ownership may not always be fully established with the operational leaders responsible for delivery.
Expectation Gap

The strategic plan is clear; the operational leaders’ daily execution ownership of it is assumed without being established through dialogue. Strategic process compliance is achieved; the internalisation of strategic intent at the execution level is not confirmed.

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.sub: Designing a shared method for establishing expectations consistently across the organisation — connecting every expectation to the future, clarifying the chain, and securing ownership through the Alignment Dialogue.
slo: Apply a consistent leadership practice for establishing expectations across the organisation.
Interpret alignment conversations to confirm genuine commitment.

parts.title: 4.1 — The Four-Step Expectation Architecture
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

The most common omission is Step 1. Leaders jump straight to the number (Step 2) and skip the Future entirely. Ask: “When you last communicated a delivery expectation, did you start with why it matters — or with what the number is?” The Future is the foundation of ownership.
content: The Expectation Architecture provides a simple, consistent method that every leader in the organisation can use — from executives to team leaders to individual contributors — to move expectations from communication into genuine ownership.
1. Start With the Future
2. Clarify the Delivery Expectation
3. Identify the Expectations Chain
4. Confirm Ownership
Begin by connecting the expectation to the organisation’s Success in Practice (SiP) — the future state the organisation is pursuing.
The objective is to help the individual understand why the expectation matters. This anchors the expectation in organisational purpose.
Example leader framing:

“As part of our goal to become the most responsive and trusted partner in our market, we need to reduce complaint response times across the service teams. This directly enables the experience we have committed to delivering to our customers.”
When expectations begin with the Future, individuals understand the contribution their work makes to the broader direction. This shifts the conversation from compliance to purpose.
Once the Future is clear, define the specific result expected — in outcome terms.
This step focuses the conversation on the result. The leader defines what success looks like in concrete, measurable terms and checks that the individual understands and shares that picture.
Example leader framing:
“The outcome we need is a reduction in resolution time from 48 hours to 12 hours by the end of Q3 2026. That is the result we are holding ourselves to: the outcome we are accountable for.”

Clarity is tested by asking the individual to describe what success looks like in their own words. If the description differs from the leader’s, the expectation requires further clarification before proceeding.
With the outcome clear, identify who else must contribute for the result to be achieved.
Most organisational outcomes depend on multiple contributors. By mapping the Expectations Chain early, the leader ensures that dependencies are visible before execution begins.
The conversation explores:
Which teams or individuals will need to collaborate on this outcome?
Whose decisions or resources directly influence the delivery of the result?
Where might coordination be required across functions?
Which external actors influence whether the result can be achieved?
This step helps the individual understand the execution system surrounding the expectation — they are not delivering alone, and the leader is confirming that the full chain has been considered.
The final step confirms that the individual accepts responsibility for ensuring the outcome is delivered. This is the moment the expectation moves from instruction to commitment.
The leader asks the Alignment Question:
“On a scale of 1–10, how aligned are you with the expectation for you to deliver this outcome?”

A score of 9 or higher indicates that the expectation has moved into genuine ownership of delivery. The leader can proceed with confidence that the individual has consciously accepted responsibility for the result.

A score below 9 means there is unresolved concern between the expectation and the individual’s readiness to own it. The leader moves immediately into the Score → Evaluate → Resolve sequence to identify and address the source of misalignment before execution begins.

parts.title: 4.2 — The Alignment Dialogue: Score → Evaluate → Resolve
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

The Resolve question — “What would move you to a 9 or 10?” — is the most important question in the whole architecture. It keeps the leader in the right posture: solving for the person’s ability to own it. Have leaders practise asking it aloud before the Application section. It sounds simple and feels unfamiliar the first time.
content: When the alignment score is below 9, the leader treats the number as data — it signals that something is unresolved. The Score → Evaluate → Resolve sequence transforms that signal into a resolved commitment.
1. Score It
2. Evaluate It
3. Resolve It
The individual provides a numerical assessment of their level of alignment. The score acts as a signal of readiness for ownership.
Score
What it signals
Leader action
9–10 | Clear ownership and readiness to deliver | Proceed; confirm the commitment and document
7–8 | Partial alignment — some uncertainty remains | Move to Evaluate → surface what is unresolved
5–6 | Significant concerns affecting confidence in delivery | Move to Evaluate → expect multiple concerns to surface
Below 5 | Expectation is not yet viable in its current form | Do not proceed — the expectation must be redesigned
If the score is below 9, the leader explores the reasons behind the rating. The objective is to understand what is preventing full alignment.
The leader guides the conversation using diagnostic questions:
“What influenced the score you gave?”
“What feels unclear about the expectation?”
“What concerns do you have about delivering this outcome?”
“Where do you anticipate obstacles or constraints?”
This step surfaces issues that might otherwise only appear during execution — when they are far more costly to resolve. Common concerns include:
Unclear definition of the outcome or success criteria
Cross-functional dependencies not yet confirmed
Capacity or resource constraints affecting feasibility
Confidence in the delivery pathway or timeline
The purpose of Evaluate is to make hidden concerns visible before execution begins.
Once the sources of misalignment are understood, the leader works with the individual to resolve them.
The guiding coaching question becomes:
“What would help move your alignment from where it is now to a 9 or 10?”
This question shifts the conversation toward solutions. Resolution may involve:
Clarifying the outcome definition or success criteria
Adjusting priorities or realistic timelines
Identifying additional support or resources required
Confirming collaboration across the Expectations Chain

Once concerns are resolved, the leader asks the alignment question again to confirm the expectation has moved into clear ownership. If it has not, the conversation continues — or the expectation itself is redesigned.
Leader’s Reflection Capture (after the dialogue):
1. Alignment Rating — Where does the commitment currently stand?
2. Primary Concern Identified — What surfaced during the discussion?
3. Action for Elevation — What will move alignment upward?

sections.label: Section 5 · Application — In Practice
sections.sub: You are a CXO establishing delivery expectations with a team member or Head of Department. Your goal is to ensure that the expectation moves beyond communication into clear ownership of delivery.
slo: Establish a delivery expectation that secures personal ownership of an agreed result.
Record the commitments that make mutual accountability visible.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Role Play Setup
Format: Pairs or triads. One person plays the CXO leader, one plays the team member/HoD, and (in triads) one observes and gives feedback. Rotate roles so each person experiences the leader position.
Timing: 15 min per round (two rounds minimum). Debrief in plenary: what felt natural, what felt unfamiliar, where the Resolve question changed the dynamic.

Key watch point: Most leaders will rush Step 1 (the Future) and the alignment question. Observers should specifically note whether the leader genuinely connected to purpose before moving to the number — and whether the Alignment Question was asked with curiosity or with pressure.
content: Case Context
Success in Practice (Future): “The most responsive and trusted partner in our market, delivering seamless execution and sustained value through collaborative excellence.”
Key Result: Cut customer complaint resolution time from 48 hours to 12 hours by Q3 2026.

parts.title: 5.1 — Step 1 · Identify Who You Are Establishing Expectations With
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
Ask participants to name one real person and role, and to state why that person is critical to the outcome.
content: Participants are asked: Before the conversation begins, clarify who holds delivery responsibility for this outcome and why their role is critical to achieving it.

parts.title: 5.2 — Step 2 · Start With the Future
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
Listen for a statement that links the expectation to the SiP future. Challenge any statement that describes a task without the future it serves.
content: Participants are asked: How would you explain why this outcome matters in relation to the SiP? This must connect the delivery expectation to the organisation’s future state.

parts.title: 5.3 — Step 3 · Clarify the Delivery Expectation
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
Check that the outcome is specific and time-bound, and that success has observable evidence. Push back on activity descriptions.
content: Participants are asked: Define the outcome clearly in result terms. Then confirm how you will verify that success has been achieved.

parts.title: 5.4 — Step 4 · Identify the Expectations Chain
guidance: 📋 PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Participants complete this activity in their own file. The content below is for your preparation.
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
Ask participants to name every contributor who influences the outcome and the coordination required. Probe for missing links in the chain.
content: Participants are asked: List the contributors who must be involved in delivering the outcome. Include upline, downline, and external chain members.
Contributor / Function
Chain Type
Role in Delivering the Outcome

parts.title: 5.5 — Step 5 · Confirm Ownership of the Result
guidance: 📋 PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Participants complete this activity in their own file. The content below is for your preparation.
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
In pairs, participants ask their ownership question and record the alignment score. Model a neutral tone: the score is data.
content: Participants are asked: How would you confirm that the individual accepts responsibility for delivering the outcome? Write your leader question, then record the alignment score.
Alignment Score

parts.title: 5.6 — Step 6 · If Alignment Is Below 9: Score → Evaluate → Resolve
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
Where scores fall below 9, coach the Evaluate → Resolve sequence. Concerns are named before actions are agreed, and a revised score is recorded.

parts.title: 5.7 — Step 7 · Leader Reflection & Commitment Record
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
Close with the reflection. Invite two or three participants to share the action agreed and what they learned about establishing expectations.
content: Participants are asked: Before concluding the conversation, capture three reflections that convert the dialogue into a visible commitment record.

parts.title: Unit Summary
guidance: ◆ Facilitator Closing Note

Close by asking each leader to name one expectation they have set but not yet established — with a specific person in their expectations chain. Ask them to commit to having that alignment dialogue within five working days and to capturing the score, the primary concern, and the action for elevation. The five-day window makes the commitment real and time-bound.
content: Awareness — What

Setting expectations communicates the required result. Establishing expectations ensures the individual understands it, can deliver it, and consciously accepts ownership of it. The Expectations Chain and Alignment Dialogue are the mechanisms that close this gap.
Intelligence — Why

Expectation alignment determines execution outcomes through five mechanisms: shifting instruction to ownership, reducing ambiguity, surfacing constraints early, strengthening accountability, and building the behavioural foundation of execution.
Extrapolating — Where

Every CXO function has a characteristic tendency to set expectations without establishing them. Without alignment dialogue, the organisation may appear aligned at the surface while engagement weakens and accountability dilutes beneath it.
Integration — Collective

The Expectation Architecture (Start with the Future → Clarify → Identify Chain → Confirm Ownership) and the Alignment Dialogue (Score → Evaluate → Resolve) create a shared leadership discipline that transforms expectation-setting into a commitment practice.
“Strong performance cultures are built by ensuring that expectations are mutually understood, realistically supported, and consciously accepted by the people responsible for delivering them.”

Accountability | Conditional; defensive ownership | Personal; proactive ownership of outcome

Think of the last time you communicated a delivery expectation. Was it set or established? How do you know?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Your Honest Assessment Think of the last time you communicated a delivery expectation. Was it set or established? How do you know? — The last expectation I communicated was... I know it was [set/established] because... What I would do differently: ...

parts.title: 1.2 — The Three Conditions of Established Expectations
content: A KPI becomes a personal leadership promise only when three conditions are simultaneously present. All three must be confirmed before execution begins.
Condition 1
Clarity — The individual understands exactly what success looks like

Clarity means understanding the full picture of the expected outcome: what must be delivered, by when, at what standard, and how success will be recognised. Most expectation conversations stop at the number. Establishing expectations requires confirming that both parties share the same picture of the result.
Test: Ask someone on your team to describe what success looks like for their key result. If the description differs from yours, clarity has not yet been established.
Condition 2
Capability — The system can realistically support delivery

Capability refers to the individual’s skill and to the system surrounding them. Are the resources, decisions, cross-functional dependencies, and coordination mechanisms in place to support delivery? A person may understand and want to own a target that the current system cannot deliver. Establishing expectations surfaces this before execution begins.
Condition 3
Commitment — The person consciously accepts ownership of the outcome

Commitment is the moment the expectation crosses from instruction to promise. The individual accepts personal responsibility for ensuring the outcome is delivered. This cannot be assumed from nodding agreement. It must be actively tested through dialogue. The Alignment Dialogue is the mechanism designed to confirm this transition has occurred.
The Alignment Dialogue asks: “On a scale of 1–10, how aligned are you with the expectation for you to deliver this outcome?” A score below 9 means Commitment is not yet established.
✎ Reflection — Which Condition Is Most Often Missing?
In your current role, which of the three conditions do you most consistently confirm — and which do you most often assume?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Which Condition Is Most Often Missing? In your current role, which of the three conditions do you most consistently confirm — and which do you most often assume? — I most consistently confirm: [Clarity / Capability / Commitment] I most often assume: ... The cost of that assumption in my last major initiative was: ...

parts.title: 1.3 — The Expectations Chain
parts.meta: Mapping who else influences the outcome
content: Very few delivery goals are achieved by a single person acting alone. The Expectations Chain identifies everyone whose work directly affects the delivery of a Key Result or KPI.
↑ Upline Chain
Those you depend on for approval, decisions, or resources
Who
Executive leadership, board members, executive sponsors, budget holders
Key question
Who must approve or resource this outcome for delivery to be possible?
↓ Downline Chain
Those responsible for executing the work to achieve the KPI
Who
Direct reports, project teams, cross-functional collaborators, shared service functions
Key question
Who must deliver specific activities for this outcome to be achieved?
↔ External Chain
External actors whose contributions influence delivery
Who
Suppliers, service partners, contractors, regulatory bodies, technology vendors
Key question
Which external actors influence whether this outcome can be delivered?
✎ Reflection — Map Your Chain
Choose one current key result. Map your Expectations Chain. Have you had an alignment dialogue with everyone in the chain — or only with the person holding the KPI?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Map Your Chain Choose one current key result. Map your Expectations Chain. Have you had an alignment dialogue with everyone in the chain — or only with the person holding the KPI? — Key Result: ... Upline: ... Downline: ... External: ... Who I have NOT yet had an alignment dialogue with: ...

parts.title: 1.4 — The Alignment Dialogue
parts.meta: Testing whether the expectation is owned
content: With the Expectations Chain mapped, the leader conducts an Alignment Dialogue with the individuals responsible for delivering the OKR/KPI. This is a structured conversation designed to test whether the expectation has moved from instruction to commitment.

The Alignment Dialogue uses a simple scale of 1–10. A score of 9 or 10 indicates genuine ownership of delivery. Anything lower demands further deliberation through the Score → Evaluate → Resolve sequence.

The power of the Alignment Dialogue lies in what the number reveals. A score of 6 is data: there is something unresolved between the expectation and the person’s readiness to own it. The leader’s job is to find it and resolve it before execution begins.

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: Why Establishing Expectations Determines Execution Outcomes
sections.sub: Understanding the five mechanisms through which expectation alignment drives ownership — and why engagement and accountability are the first two casualties when this step is skipped.
slo: Explain how establishing expectations builds ownership and mutual accountability.
Recognise how engagement and accountability degrade when expectations are only communicated.

parts.title: 2.1 — Compliance vs Commitment: The Execution Dynamic
content: The moment when expectations are clarified between leader and contributor is the moment a performance target transitions from organisational intention to personal responsibility. If that transition does not occur, execution becomes fragile regardless of how well the system has been designed.
Dimension
Compliance-Driven
Commitment-Driven
When obstacles arise | Escalate upward; remain cautious; protect reporting | Take initiative; surface issues early; co-design solutions
Accountability | Activity ownership — responsible for tasks | Outcome ownership — personally accountable for the result
Energy | Reserved; discretionary effort withheld | Fully invested; discretionary effort freely given
How it sounds | “I completed everything that was asked of me.” | “I’ll make sure this gets delivered.”
✎ Reflection — Your Team Right Now
When your team hits an unexpected obstacle, what happens first — do they solve it, or do they escalate it? What does the answer tell you about the execution dynamic you have created?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Your Team Right Now When your team hits an unexpected obstacle, what happens first — do they solve it, or do they escalate it? What does the answer tell you about the execution dynamic you have created? — When my team hits an obstacle, the typical response is... This suggests the execution dynamic is closer to [compliance/commitment] because... The expectation conversation that would shift this: ...

parts.title: 2.2 — Five Mechanisms: Why Expectation Alignment Determines Outcomes
content: Mechanism 1
From Instruction to Ownership

When expectations are merely communicated, people interpret them as instructions. They understand what must be achieved but do not yet feel personally accountable for ensuring the outcome is delivered. Structured dialogue moves the individual from acknowledging the requirement to accepting ownership of the result.
Mechanism 2
Reducing Interpretation Ambiguity

Individuals interpret what success requires differently depending on their role, expertise, and operational context. Without alignment, people may pursue the same goal while working from different assumptions. Establishing expectations creates a shared interpretation of what must be delivered, why it matters, and how success will be recognised.
Mechanism 3
Surfacing Constraints Before Execution Begins

If dependencies are not identified during the expectation conversation, they only become visible later — often when deadlines are approaching. Establishing expectations allows leaders and contributors to identify cross-functional dependencies, resource needs, and potential risks before they become execution crises.
Mechanism 4
Strengthening Accountability

Accountability is strongest when individuals perceive that expectations placed on them are clear, achievable, and meaningful. Establishing expectations ensures both parties share a common understanding of the responsibility involved, the support available, and the standards for evaluating success — transforming accountability from formal obligation to shared commitment.
Mechanism 5
Building the Behavioural Foundation

Strategy execution is fundamentally a behavioural challenge. Establishing performance expectations ensures that individuals are psychologically prepared to take responsibility for doing it. When this foundation is in place, purpose is understood, confidence increases, collaboration improves, and accountability becomes proactive.
✎ Reflection — Your Most Absent Mechanism
Which of the five mechanisms is most absent in your current execution environment? What is the cost of that absence right now?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Your Most Absent Mechanism Which of the five mechanisms is most absent in your current execution environment? What is the cost of that absence right now? — The mechanism most absent is Mechanism ___ because... The cost I can see in my organisation: ... The conversation I need to have: ...

parts.title: 2.3 — Engagement & Accountability: The Two Casualties
parts.meta: What breaks down when expectations are only set
content: First Casualty
Engagement Weakens — Observable but Subtle
Work progresses, but discretionary effort is limited
Individuals wait for direction and leave emerging problems unaddressed
Cross-functional coordination slows; people focus on their own responsibilities
Engagement becomes transactional — roles are performed, collective ownership does not materialise
Signal: work is happening, but energy is not invested. People are present but not propelled.
Critical Long-Term Impact
Accountability Dilutes — The Deeper Cost
Performance discussions revolve around explanations
Conversations focus on constraints
Cross-functional dependencies create delays because responsibility for resolving them is unclear
Multiple teams feel partially responsible; none is fully accountable

The paradox: teams appear to be working hard, meetings are frequent, updates are detailed — yet the organisation consistently struggles to achieve what it set out to deliver. The issue is that ownership was assigned without being secured.

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.h2: Where Does the Expectations Gap Emerge?
sections.sub: Examining how each executive function’s natural tendency creates a characteristic expectation gap — and why surface alignment so often conceals unresolved ownership.
slo: Identify where each executive function tends to set expectations without securing ownership.
Recognise when surface agreement masks unresolved ownership.

parts.title: 3.1 — The Alignment Brigade: CXO Expectation Tendencies & Gaps
content: Each executive function communicates expectations through the mechanisms it controls. Click your role to explore your typical tendency and the gap it creates. Then explore the two roles most adjacent to yours.
CEO
Enterprise Ambition
CFO
Financial Precision
COO
Operational Discipline
CHRO
Cultural Alignment
CTO/CIO
Technical Milestones
CMO
Market Performance
CCO
Commercial Ambition
CPO
Procurement Discipline
CRO
Risk Governance
CSO
Strategic Planning
Typical Tendency

Often sets enterprise ambition and directional expectations, assuming functional leaders will translate these into delivery realities. The strategic signal is clear, but the conditions required for execution may not be fully established through dialogue.
The Expectation Gap

Functional leaders receive strategic direction clearly yet lack confirmed ownership of the conditions required for delivery. The assumption that strategic clarity cascades automatically into execution commitment is the CEO’s most common expectation gap.
Reflection: What is an enterprise-level expectation you have communicated recently? Have you established the conditions for delivery with the leaders responsible?
Typical Tendency

Frequently sets precise financial performance expectations through budgets, targets, and reporting timelines. Financial clarity is strong, yet the cross-functional conditions required to deliver financial outcomes may not be fully established with teams responsible for operational delivery.
The Expectation Gap

The finance number is clear; the ownership of delivering it is not. Teams understand the target but may not have confirmed the cross-functional conditions — resources, decisions, capacity — required to achieve it.
Reflection: Who in your expectations chain holds a financial target they received from you? Have you confirmed they own the conditions for delivery?
Typical Tendency

Commonly sets operational expectations through processes, service levels, and execution discipline. Operational clarity is high, though alignment conversations that build emotional commitment and shared ownership may receive less attention.
The Expectation Gap
Process compliance is achieved; outcome ownership is not. Teams follow the operational procedure without necessarily feeling personally responsible for whether the broader result is delivered.
Reflection: Which operational expectation in your area is being executed compliantly but not yet owned?
Typical Tendency

Often sets expectations around people behaviour, engagement, and cultural alignment. The dialogue is typically strong on social and emotional commitment, while the direct linkage to operational and commercial delivery expectations may require further clarification.
The Expectation Gap
People feel culturally aligned but may not have clear delivery commitments. Engagement is high; the connection between that engagement and measurable commercial outcomes may remain under-established.
Reflection: Where does your people agenda connect most directly to a commercial delivery expectation? Is that connection established with both parties?
Typical Tendency

Frequently sets delivery expectations through technical specifications, system milestones, and project timelines. Technical clarity is strong, though broader organisational alignment around how technology outcomes enable business delivery may require deeper dialogue.
The Expectation Gap

The technical milestone is clear; the business owner’s commitment to using the technology outcome to deliver the result is not established. Technology delivers; business ownership of the enabled result is assumed without confirmation.
Reflection: Which technology outcome have you delivered recently that was not fully converted into business value? What expectation conversation was missing?
Typical Tendency

Often sets market growth or brand performance expectations through campaign metrics and positioning targets. These expectations frequently depend on multiple functions for delivery, yet the cross-functional support commitments required may not always be fully established.
The Expectation Gap

The campaign target is clear; the operational and commercial functions have not confirmed their ownership of enabling the marketing outcome. Market expectations are set with marketing; the chain extending to other functions remains under-established.
Reflection: Which functions are critical to your marketing outcomes? Have you established expectations with them?
Typical Tendency

Commonly sets ambitious commercial expectations to drive revenue momentum and market urgency. Stretch targets are clear, although the operational conditions required to sustain those outcomes may not be fully aligned across the organisation.
The Expectation Gap

The commercial target is understood; the operational capacity to deliver it sustainably is not confirmed. Revenue commitments are made without fully establishing whether the operational expectations chain has been aligned to support them.
Reflection: What is the most ambitious commercial target you currently carry? Have you established the operational expectations chain required to sustain it?
Typical Tendency

Often sets procurement expectations through contractual terms, supplier metrics, and compliance frameworks. These mechanisms create discipline with external partners, though internal alignment required to convert procurement outcomes into enterprise value may need further establishment.
The Expectation Gap

Supplier expectations are clear; internal expectations for converting supplier performance into business value are not established. The internal expectations chain for converting inputs into outcomes remains under-confirmed.
Reflection: Which procurement outcome is delivering inputs that are not yet being converted into enterprise value? What internal alignment conversation is missing?
Typical Tendency

Frequently sets expectations for risk control and compliance through governance frameworks, policies, and reporting standards. Rules are clear, yet deeper organisational ownership of risk-aware behaviour may require additional dialogue to move beyond procedural compliance.
The Expectation Gap

The governance rule is understood; the ownership of risk-aware behaviour remains procedural. Compliance is achieved; commitment to risk-aware decision-making as a shared organisational responsibility is not established.
Reflection: Where in your organisation is risk compliance still only procedural? What alignment conversation would change this?
Typical Tendency

Often sets expectations around planning milestones, strategic reviews, and OKR cycles. Strategic process discipline is strong, though expectations for day-to-day execution ownership may not always be fully established with the operational leaders responsible.
The Expectation Gap

The strategic plan is clear; operational leaders’ daily execution ownership of it is assumed without being established through dialogue. Strategic process compliance is achieved; internalisation of strategic intent at execution level is not confirmed.
Reflection: Which operational leaders have received your strategic plan but not yet accepted ownership of delivering it? What is one alignment conversation you need to have this week?
✎ Reflection — Your Expectation Gap
Based on your role exploration: what is the most important expectation you have set but not yet established? Who in your chain needs that alignment dialogue?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Your Expectation Gap Based on your role exploration: what is the most important expectation you have set but not yet established? Who in your chain needs that alignment dialogue? — The expectation I have set but not established: ... The person/function I need to establish it with: ... The alignment dialogue I will have within 5 working days: ...

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.sub: A shared leadership practice for establishing expectations consistently across the organisation — from the Future to the Alignment Dialogue.
slo: Apply a consistent leadership practice for establishing expectations across the organisation.
Interpret alignment conversations to confirm genuine commitment.

parts.title: 4.1 — The Four-Step Expectation Architecture
content: Step 1
Start With the Future
Purpose
Connect the expectation to the organisation’s Success in Practice — so the individual understands why the outcome matters.
Leader framing
“As part of our goal to become the most responsive partner in our market, we need to reduce complaint response times across the service teams.”
Why it matters
When expectations begin with the Future, individuals understand the contribution their work makes to the broader direction. This shifts the conversation from compliance to purpose.
Step 2
Clarify the Delivery Expectation
Purpose
Define the specific outcome required — in result terms. Confirm a shared picture of what success looks like.
Leader framing
“The outcome we need is a reduction in resolution time from 48 hours to 12 hours by Q3 2026.”
Why it matters
Clarity is tested by asking the individual to describe success in their own words. If the description differs from yours, clarify further before proceeding.
Step 3
Identify the Expectations Chain
Purpose
Map who else must contribute for the result to be achieved. Ensure dependencies are visible before execution begins.
Explore
Which teams must collaborate? Whose decisions influence delivery? Where might coordination be required? Which external actors are involved?
Why it matters
This step helps the individual understand the execution system surrounding the expectation — they are not delivering alone.
Step 4
Confirm Ownership of the Result
Purpose
Confirm that the individual accepts responsibility for ensuring the outcome is delivered. This is the moment the expectation moves from instruction to commitment.
The question
“On a scale of 1–10, how aligned are you with the expectation for you to deliver this outcome?”
What it means
9–10 = proceed with confidence. Below 9 = move to Score → Evaluate → Resolve before execution begins.
✎ Reflection — Which Step Do You Most Often Skip?
Of the four steps, which one do you most often move through too quickly? What would change if you gave it more time?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Which Step Do You Most Often Skip? Of the four steps, which one do you most often move through too quickly? What would change if you gave it more time? — I most often rush Step ___ because... If I gave it more time, I would: ...

parts.title: 4.2 — The Alignment Dialogue: Score → Evaluate → Resolve
content: When the alignment score is below 9, the leader does not challenge the score or move past it. The number is data. The Score → Evaluate → Resolve sequence transforms that signal into a resolved commitment.
Score It
The individual provides their alignment number — a signal of readiness
Score | Signal | Your action
9–10 | Clear ownership; ready to deliver | Proceed; confirm and document
7–8 | Partial alignment — uncertainty remains | Move to Evaluate
5–6 | Significant concerns affecting confidence | Move to Evaluate; expect multiple concerns
Below 5 | Expectation not viable in current form | Do not proceed — redesign the expectation
Evaluate It
Understand what is preventing full alignment
The leader explores the reasons behind the score to understand it. Use diagnostic questions:
“What influenced the score you gave?”
“What feels unclear about the expectation?”
“What concerns do you have about delivering this outcome?”
“Where do you anticipate obstacles or constraints?”
Common concerns that surface: unclear outcome definition, cross-functional dependencies not confirmed, capacity or resource constraints, confidence in the delivery pathway or timeline.
Resolve It
Work with the individual to resolve the concern
“What would help move your alignment from where it is now to a 9 or 10?”

This question shifts the conversation toward solutions. Resolution may involve: clarifying the outcome, adjusting priorities or timelines, identifying additional support, confirming collaboration across the chain. Once resolved, ask the alignment question again to confirm ownership has been established.
After the dialogue, capture three reflections:
1. Alignment Rating — Where does commitment stand?
2. Primary Concern Identified — What surfaced?
3. Action for Elevation — What will move alignment upward?
✎ Reflection — Practise the Resolve Question
Write the Resolve question in your own words. Then apply it to a real expectation alignment scenario you are currently facing.
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Practise the Resolve Question Write the Resolve question in your own words. Then apply it to a real expectation alignment scenario you are currently facing. — The Resolve question in my own words: “...” Applied to my current situation: if I asked this of [person], I would expect them to say... And I would respond by: ...
